title: Episode 83: Robert Smalls and the Stealing of the CSS Planter: The Midnight Voyage to Freedom
description:
Robert Smalls and the Stealing of the CSS Planter: The Midnight Voyage to Freedom. How an enslaved harbor pilot commandeered a Confederate gunship, navigated past five fortified rebel island forts in May 1862, and delivered his family and military secrets to the Union blockade. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into one of the most audacious acts of courage in American history.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the pitch black of 3:00 AM on May 13, 1862, in the heavily fortified Confederate stronghold of Charleston harbor, an act of supreme courage was set into motion. Robert Smalls, a thirty-three-year-old enslaved maritime pilot, quietly boarded the CSS Planter—an armed Confederate paddlewheel gunboat loaded with cannons, ammunition, and top-secret harbor signaling codes. With the white officers asleep ashore in violation of orders, Smalls, his fellow enslaved crewmen, and their families quietly cast off lines. Donning the captain's trademark straw hat and coat to disguise his silhouette in the darkness, Smalls piloted the warship past five Confederate island forts, blowing the proper whistle signals to sentinel guards, and steamed straight for the Union blockade. George brings us the breathtaking true story of Robert Smalls.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ENSLAVED HELMSMAN OF THE LOWCOUNTRY
Born into slavery in eighteen thirty-nine in the coastal town of Beaufort, South Carolina, Robert Smalls was a man of extraordinary natural intellect, physical presence, and maritime aptitude. Taken to Charleston as a youth by his owner, Smalls worked along the bustling harbor wharves as a lamplighter, sailmaker, and dock rigger before becoming a steersman on coastal transport vessels. Smalls possessed an encyclopedic, photographic memory of Charleston harbor's treacherous waterways: he mastered every winding tidal channel, submerged sandbar, coral shoal, and shifting current from Georgetown down to Savannah. When the Civil War erupted in eighteen sixty-one, the Confederate navy eagerly hired Smalls as the chief helmsman aboard the CSS Planter, a brand-new, three-hundred-ton wood-burning paddlewheel steamship. Measuring one hundred and forty feet long, the Planter was the personal dispatch boat and armed transport of Confederate Brigadier General Roswell Ripley, used to inspect fortifications and transport heavy artillery between harbor island forts. Though white officers officially held command, it was the enslaved Robert Smalls who actually steered the ship through the labyrinthine coastal defenses. Smalls was respected by white captains for his extraordinary navigational instincts, capable of steering heavy paddlewheelers through pitch-black channels and blinding coastal fog without ever running aground. Smalls understood the tides, shoals, and wind patterns of Charleston harbor with consummate mastery, navigating narrow shipping channels that baffled veteran naval officers and earning the respect of harbor merchants.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE PLAN IN THE SHADOWS
Smalls was deeply devoted to his wife, Hannah, and their two young children, but lived in constant agony knowing that as enslaved people, his family could be sold down the river to distant Louisiana plantations at any moment. Smalls had attempted to purchase his family's freedom for eight hundred dollars, but had saved only a fraction of the astronomical sum. In early May eighteen sixty-two, an extraordinary opportunity presented itself. The Confederate high command was consolidating artillery, and the Planter took aboard four heavy cannons to transport to Fort Ripley: a thirty-two-pounder pivot gun on the bow, a massive forty-two-pounder banded rifle, and an eight-inch howitzer, along with two hundred pounds of gunpowder. Smalls recognized that the armed warship was a floating fortress and a priceless military prize. Gathering his six fellow enslaved crewmen in the ship's cramped engine room, Smalls laid out his plan: if the white officers ever left the ship overnight, they would steal the vessel, pick up their wives and children hidden aboard a nearby wharf boat, and steam straight for the federal blockade fleet outside the harbor. The crew understood the stakes: if captured, they would be tortured and hanged as insurrectionists. They swore an unbreakable pact: if discovered, they would blow up the ship's boiler and die free together in the harbor. Hannah Smalls looked into her husband eyes on the eve of the escape and said with unshakeable courage: It is a risk, dear, but you and I, and our little children, must go with you. Where you die, I will die. The enslaved crew members gathered in secret in the ship hold, whispering prayers and reviewing the escape route, fully aware that a single suspicious look from a sentry would mean death on the gallows.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: CASTING OFF UNDER THE SOUTHERN CROSS
On the evening of Monday, May twelfth, eighteen sixty-two, fortune favored the brave. Captain Charles Relyea and his two white officers violated strict military orders by leaving the Planter tied to the Southern Wharf while they went ashore to sleep in the city. At two o'clock in the morning on May thirteenth, Smalls acted. He ordered the boiler fires stoked quietly with pine wood, hoisted the Confederate stars and bars and the South Carolina state flag to deceive shore lookouts, and donned Captain Relyea's wide-brimmed straw hat and heavy frock coat, mimicking the captain's peculiar gait. At three AM, Smalls gave the order to cast off mooring lines. Backing smoothly into the harbor, Smalls steered the Planter to the nearby Atlantic Wharf, where Hannah Smalls, their children, and four other enslaved women and children were trembling in the hold of an old barge. Moving silently in the darkness, the families boarded the gunboat, tears streaming down Hannah's face as she clutched her infant son to her chest, whispering prayers into the cool night air. Smalls had studied Captain Relyea posture for months, practicing folding his arms and leaning casually against the pilot house rail so that sentries watching through telescopes from shore would suspect nothing. The paddlewheels churned quietly in the dark water as the Planter slipped away from the wharf, moving with ghostly silence past sleeping Confederate sentries and anchored harbor patrol boats.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TEST OF FORT SUMTER
Steaming down the main ship channel toward the open sea, the Planter had to pass five heavily armed Confederate island forts: Fort Johnson, Fort Ripley, Castle Pinckney, Battery Marion, and the towering brick fortress of Fort Sumter, whose massive gun emplacements commanded the narrow harbor entrance. At four fifteen AM, in the pre-dawn gray, the Planter glided directly beneath the imposing brick ramparts of Fort Sumter. Sentinels with loaded muskets paced the parapets barely three hundred yards away. Smalls knew that if he sped up or showed hesitation, the fort's forty-two-pounder coastal guns would blow the wooden steamship out of the water in seconds. Standing calmly in the wheelhouse with his back turned to the fort, arms folded like Captain Relyea, Smalls reached up and pulled the steam whistle cord: three sharp blasts and one long blast—the secret Confederate naval recognition signal. On the ramparts above, the Confederate sentry watched the familiar outline of the General's dispatch boat pass into the morning mist, shouting to his officer: 'The Planter is going out early this morning!' As the Planter glided past the dark silhouette of Fort Sumter, the enslaved crewmen held their breath, clutching their revolvers in silence and ready to ignite the boiler if the sentry ordered the batteries to open fire. Smalls blew the whistle blasts with flawless timing, mimicking Captain Relyea customary cadence so perfectly that the Confederate officers on Fort Sumter never doubted the identity of the vessel.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE WHITE SHEET OF SURRENDER
The moment the Planter cleared the range of Fort Sumter's rear guns, Smalls opened the throttle valve to maximum speed. The paddlewheels churned the water into foam as the vessel raced toward the federal blockade line, four miles offshore. Just as the sun broke over the Atlantic horizon, Confederate lookouts on Morris Island realized the ship was steaming past the outer channel buoys without stopping. Confederate alarm guns boomed from Sumter, but it was too late: the Planter was beyond their range. Now a new, deadly danger arose: the Union blockade fleet. Spotting an armed Confederate gunboat bearing down on them at full speed with rebel flags flying, the crew of the USS Onward—a heavily armed naval clipper ship—swung her port guns into battery, preparing to fire a devastating broadside of explosive shells into the approaching vessel. Hannah Smalls rushed forward with a white bedsheet she had brought from home. Smalls hauled down the Confederate flags, hoisted the white sheet to the masthead, and threw his straw hat into the sea. Seeing the white flag of surrender, the captain of the Onward held his fire at the absolute last second. The crew of the USS Onward were astonished to see the Confederate warship round the headland and haul down the rebel flag, replacing it with a white bedsheet that fluttered peacefully in the morning sun. When the Union sailors on the USS Onward spotted the white bedsheet, cheers erupted across the warship as the crew realized an enslaved pilot had accomplished the impossible right under the enemy guns.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: DELIVERING AN EMPIRE'S SECRETS
As the Onward's armed boarding party rowed alongside, Robert Smalls stepped to the railing, saluted the naval officer, and shouted with tears of triumph in his eyes: 'Good morning, sir! I have brought you some of the United States guns, sir!' The Union navy could barely believe their eyes: an enslaved helmsman had delivered an intact Confederate warship, four heavy coastal cannons, two hundred pounds of ammunition, sixteen liberated souls, and Captain Relyea's confidential signal book containing all the secret Confederate naval codes and harbor mine maps for Charleston and Savannah! Rear Admiral Samuel Francis Du Pont hailed Smalls's feat as one of the most brilliant and heroic naval exploits of the entire war. The United States Congress passed a special bill signed by President Abraham Lincoln awarding Smalls and his crew fifteen hundred dollars in prize money—a fortune at the time. Lincoln invited Smalls to the White House, where Smalls passionately persuaded the president and Secretary of War Edwin Stanton to allow African American men to enlist in the Union armed forces, directly leading to the formation of the historic United States Colored Troops. Admiral Du Pont immediately recognized the strategic brilliance of Smalls feat, writing to the Secretary of the Navy that the captured charts and signal codes were of incalculable value to the Union war effort. President Lincoln recognized Smalls extraordinary bravery as a turning point in the war, citing his daring escape as undeniable proof of the courage, patriotism, and military capability of Black Americans.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE STATESMAN OF BEAUFORT
Robert Smalls was commissioned as a pilot and later promoted to full captain in the United States Navy—the first African American naval captain in American history—commanding the USS Planter in seventeen naval engagements throughout the remainder of the war. Following the Confederate surrender, Smalls returned as a free man to his hometown of Beaufort, South Carolina. In an astonishing act of poetic justice, Smalls used his naval prize money to purchase the grand antebellum mansion where he had once been enslaved, allowing his former owner's elderly, destitute widow to live out her remaining days in peace in her former home. Smalls went on to serve five terms in the United States House of Representatives, authored the legislation creating South Carolina's public school system, and served as collector of customs at Beaufort for two decades. Today, a statue of Robert Smalls stands proudly in Beaufort, and a naval warship, the USNS Robert Smalls, sails the oceans of the world, honoring the enslaved pilot whose midnight courage carried sixteen souls through the jaws of death to freedom. Robert Smalls lived out his remarkable life as an American hero, championing voting rights and public education in Congress, and proving that an enslaved man from the Lowcountry could rise to become a founding father of American civil rights. Robert Smalls historic voyage aboard the Planter remains one of the greatest tales of liberation in human history, an immortal testament to the unquenchable human spirit that risks everything for freedom.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Robert Smalls proved that the thirst for freedom could outmaneuver the fortress cannons of an empire. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey to Richmond, Virginia, for the sensational treason trial of former Vice President Aaron Burr.
